redis-model.tldr:
• One thread executes commands, so each command is atomic; I/O threads only handle networking.
  • One slow command (KEYS *, huge HGETALL, big DEL) blocks every client.
  • Use SCAN and UNLINK, keep values small.
  • Scale with sharding (Cluster), not threads.
redis-model.body:
Redis is an in-memory data structure server. Speed comes from: data in RAM; efficient encodings (listpack, intset, skiplist); a single-threaded command executor (no locks, no context switches) driven by an event loop with I/O multiplexing (epoll); and a simple protocol (RESP).

A typical command costs microseconds of CPU: the bottleneck is almost always the network round trip (~100–500 µs in a data centre), which is why pipelining and batching (MGET, HMGET) matter more than server tuning.

  • Each command runs atomically: no other command interleaves with it. That's why INCR needs no lock.
  • Since Redis 6, I/O threads (io-threads) can parallelize socket reads/writes and protocol parsing; command execution stays single-threaded. Background threads handle UNLINK, AOF fsync and lazy freeing.
  • Because one thread executes everything, one slow command blocks all clients: KEYS *, SMEMBERS on a million-element set, HGETALL on huge hashes, DEL of a big key, FLUSHALL. Use SCAN/HSCAN/SSCAN, UNLINK (async delete) and keep values small.

Interview tip "single-threaded" is about command execution. It scales up with sharding (Redis Cluster) or multiple instances per machine, not by adding threads.

Redis vs Memcached: Redis has rich data structures, persistence, replication, clustering, Lua scripting, pub/sub and streams; Memcached is a multi-threaded, simple key-value cache. Licensing note: Redis moved to source-available licences in 2024 (AGPL added as an option in Redis 8); the Linux Foundation fork Valkey is API-compatible and is used by several cloud providers.

redis-structures.tldr:
• Strings for values/counters/locks, hashes for objects, lists for queues, sets for uniqueness.
  • Sorted sets power leaderboards, delayed jobs and sliding windows.
  • HyperLogLog counts uniques in 12 KB; streams give consumer groups with acks.
  • Name keys service:entity:id, set TTLs on cache keys, avoid big keys.
redis-structures.body:
Type Commands Use cases Complexity
String SET, GET, INCR, SETEX, MGET cache values, counters, locks, sessions O(1)
Hash HSET, HGET, HINCRBY, HGETALL object fields (user profile), per-field updates O(1) per field
List LPUSH, RPOP, BLPOP, LRANGE queues, recent items, timelines O(1) ends
Set SADD, SISMEMBER, SINTER, SCARD unique tags, followers, dedup O(1) membership
Sorted set (ZSET) ZADD, ZINCRBY, ZRANGE ... REV, ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboards, priority queues, sliding windows, delayed jobs O(log n)
Bitmap SETBIT, BITCOUNT daily active users, feature flags per user id O(1)
HyperLogLog PFADD, PFCOUNT approximate unique counts (0.81% error, 12 KB) O(1)
Geo GEOADD, GEOSEARCH nearby drivers/stores O(log n)
Stream XADD, XREADGROUP, XACK, XPENDING durable event log with consumer groups O(1) append
Shell
# Leaderboard
ZADD game:scores 1500 "nk" 1320 "asha" 1710 "ravi"
ZINCRBY game:scores 50 "nk"
ZRANGE game:scores 0 9 REV WITHSCORES        # top 10
ZREVRANK game:scores "nk"                    # 0-based rank

# Counter with expiry (fixed-window rate limit)
INCR rl:user42:202610211530
EXPIRE rl:user42:202610211530 60

# Unique visitors today
PFADD uv:2026-10-21 user1 user2 user3
PFCOUNT uv:2026-10-21

# Delayed job queue: score = run-at epoch seconds
ZADD jobs:delayed 1761040800 "job:9812"
ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs:delayed 0 1761040800 LIMIT 0 100

How Redis stores them — encodings switch automatically

Type Small (memory-compact) Large (fast for big sizes) Threshold (default)
Hash listpack (flat array) hashtable > 128 fields or value > 64 bytes
Set intset (sorted ints) / listpack hashtable > 512 members
Sorted set listpack skiplist + hashtable > 128 members or value > 64 bytes
List listpack quicklist (linked list of listpacks) per-node size
String int / embstr (≤ 44 bytes) raw SDS —

OBJECT ENCODING key shows the encoding. Storing an object as one hash with small fields is far more memory-efficient than many separate string keys — the reason for the "bucket hashes" trick (HSET user:bucket:42 4217 ...) used at scale.

Why a sorted set is a skiplist + hash table

Key naming: service:entity:id[:field] (e.g. order:cart:42). Keep keys short but readable, always set TTLs on cache keys, and avoid big keys (> ~1 MB strings, collections > ~10k elements) because they block the thread on read/delete and unbalance cluster slots.

redis-persistence.tldr:
• RDB snapshots are compact but lose recent writes; AOF everysec loses at most ~1 s.
  • The hybrid (RDB preamble + AOF) is the usual production choice.
  • fork() for snapshots can spike memory via copy-on-write.
  • A pure cache may run without persistence.

redis-eviction.tldr:
• Keys expire lazily on access and actively by sampling.
  • maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru/allkeys-lfu for caches; noeviction makes writes fail when full.
  • volatile-* policies only evict keys with TTLs.
  • LRU/LFU are approximated by sampling.
redis-eviction.body:
Expiry: EXPIRE, SET key val EX 60, PERSIST. Redis removes expired keys lazily (when accessed) and actively (a background cycle samples keys with TTLs). So memory isn't freed exactly at expiry.

Eviction happens when maxmemory is reached:

Policy Evicts
noeviction (default) nothing; writes fail with OOM error
allkeys-lru least recently used among all keys (typical cache)
allkeys-lfu least frequently used among all keys (hot sets)
volatile-lru / volatile-lfu LRU/LFU among keys with a TTL
allkeys-random / volatile-random random
volatile-ttl keys with the shortest remaining TTL

LRU/LFU are approximated by sampling (maxmemory-samples, default 5) rather than tracking perfect order.

LFU keeps an 8-bit logarithmic access counter per key that decays over time (lfu-decay-time), so yesterday's hot key eventually becomes evictable. Prefer allkeys-lfu for caches with a stable hot set, allkeys-lru for recency-driven access.

Config
maxmemory 4gb
maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu

Pitfall using volatile-* while most keys have no TTL leaves nothing evictable, and writes start failing like noeviction.

redis-ha.tldr:
• Replication is asynchronous; WAIT reduces but doesn't remove loss on failover.
  • Sentinel provides failover for one primary; Cluster adds sharding over 16384 hash slots.
  • Multi-key operations in Cluster need hash tags ({user:42}).
  • Choose Cluster when data or writes exceed one node.

redis-caching.tldr:
• Cache-aside: read cache, load DB on miss, write DB then delete the key after commit.
  • Delete rather than update the cache to avoid ordering races.
  • Add TTL jitter; consider a small local cache in front for very hot keys.
  • Write-through and write-behind trade write latency against durability.

redis-failures.tldr:
• Penetration (missing keys): cache nulls briefly, Bloom filter.
  • Breakdown (one hot key expires): mutex rebuild or logical expiry.
  • Avalanche (mass expiry or outage): TTL jitter, HA Redis, protect the DB.
  • Cache and DB consistency is eventual; don't cache what must be strongly consistent.
redis-failures.body:
Cache penetration — requests for keys that don't exist anywhere (often malicious ids) miss the cache every time and hit the DB.

A Bloom filter never gives false negatives, only (tunable, ~1%) false positives, so it can safely reject ids that were never created. Add each new id to the filter on insert.

Fixes: cache the negative result (product:999 = NULL with a short TTL); validate input; a Bloom filter of existing ids in front of the cache (RedisBloom BF.EXISTS).

Cache breakdown (hotspot invalid / thundering herd / stampede) — a single hot key expires and thousands of concurrent requests all miss and hammer the DB.

Logical expiry avoids even the waiting: store {value, expiresAt} without a Redis TTL; a reader that sees an expired value returns it anyway and lets one thread (holding the lock) refresh in the background.

Fixes: a mutex so only one request rebuilds; logical expiry (keep serving the stale value while one thread refreshes); never-expiring hot keys refreshed in the background; probabilistic early refresh.

Java
public Product getWithMutex(long id) throws Exception {
    String key = "product:" + id, lockKey = "lock:" + key;
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < 50; attempt++) {
        String v = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
        if (v != null) return json.readValue(v, Product.class);

        String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        Boolean locked = redis.opsForValue().setIfAbsent(lockKey, token, Duration.ofSeconds(5));
        if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(locked)) {
            try {
                String again = redis.opsForValue().get(key);                 // double-check
                if (again != null) return json.readValue(again, Product.class);
                Product p = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
                redis.opsForValue().set(key, json.writeValueAsString(p), Duration.ofMinutes(30));
                return p;
            } finally {
                releaseLock(lockKey, token);                                 // Lua compare-and-delete
            }
        }
        Thread.sleep(50);                                                    // someone else is rebuilding
    }
    return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();                                  // give up waiting; go to DB
}

Cache avalanche — many keys expire at the same time (all loaded at startup with the same TTL) or the Redis cluster goes down, and the DB is flooded.

Fixes: TTL jitter; staggered warm-up; HA Redis (replicas, Cluster); circuit breaker and rate limiting in front of the DB; local cache fallback.

Problem Trigger Key fix
Penetration non-existent keys cache nulls, Bloom filter
Breakdown one hot key expires mutex rebuild / logical expiry
Avalanche mass expiry or Redis down TTL jitter, HA, circuit breaker

Consistency between cache and DB is always eventual. For strong requirements (balances, stock), read the DB or use the cache only as an optimization with short TTLs.

redis-locks.tldr:
• Acquire with SET key token NX PX ttl; release with a Lua compare-and-delete.
  • Redisson adds a watchdog that renews leases, plus reentrant and fair locks.
  • Failover and long pauses can break mutual exclusion: add fencing for correctness.
  • Keep the lock scope minimal.

redis-atomic.tldr:
• MULTI/EXEC runs commands together with no rollback; WATCH adds optimistic checks.
  • Lua scripts give atomic check-and-set logic; keep them short.
  • Pipelining cuts round trips but isn't atomic.
  • Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget; Streams persist with consumer groups.
redis-atomic.body:
MULTI/EXEC queues commands and runs them together without interleaving. There's no rollback: if a command fails at runtime, the others still run. WATCH adds optimistic locking: EXEC aborts if a watched key changed.

Which atomicity tool?

Need Tool
one command on one key it's already atomic (INCR, SET NX, HINCRBY)
several writes, no reads in between, no logic MULTI/EXEC (or pipeline + MULTI)
read → decide → write, low contention WATCH + MULTI/EXEC, retry on nil
read → decide → write, any contention Lua script / Function
many independent commands fast pipelining (not atomic)
Shell
WATCH stock:sku1
GET stock:sku1          # client checks the value
MULTI
DECRBY stock:sku1 2
LPUSH orders:queue "o-77"
EXEC                    # returns nil if stock:sku1 changed since WATCH -> retry

Lua scripts (EVAL, or Redis 7 Functions) run atomically on the server with logic and conditionals — the usual tool for check-and-set operations.

Lua
-- Atomic stock decrement: returns remaining stock, or -1 if insufficient
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local qty = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if stock < qty then return -1 end
return redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
Lua
-- Sliding-window rate limiter on a sorted set
-- KEYS[1] = key, ARGV[1] = now ms, ARGV[2] = window ms, ARGV[3] = limit, ARGV[4] = unique member
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1] - ARGV[2])
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count < tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
  redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[4])
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
  return 1
end
return 0

Keep scripts short: they block the server while running.

Pipelining sends many commands without waiting for each reply, cutting round trips (not atomic).

Java
List<Object> results = redis.executePipelined((RedisCallback<Object>) conn -> {
    for (long id : ids) conn.stringCommands().get(("product:" + id).getBytes());
    return null;
});

Each group tracks its own position; each message is delivered to one consumer in the group and stays in that consumer's pending entries list (PEL) until XACK. Messages stuck in the PEL of a dead consumer are reclaimed with XAUTOCLAIM — that's how Streams give at-least-once delivery.

Pub/Sub vs Streams

Pub/Sub Streams
Delivery fire-and-forget to currently connected subscribers persisted log
Offline consumers miss messages read later from an ID
Consumer groups / acks no yes (XREADGROUP, XACK, XPENDING, XCLAIM)
Use cache invalidation broadcasts, live notifications lightweight job queues, event logs
Shell
XADD orders * orderId 42 status PLACED
XGROUP CREATE orders billing $ MKSTREAM
XREADGROUP GROUP billing worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders >
XACK orders billing 1761040800000-0

redis-ratelimit.tldr:
• Fixed windows allow 2× bursts at boundaries; sliding window counters fix that with two integers.
  • Token bucket allows short bursts up to capacity while enforcing an average rate — the common production choice.
  • Do check-and-consume in one Lua script so concurrent instances can't race.
  • Decide fail-open vs fail-closed per limit, and return 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit headers.
redis-ratelimit.body:
A shared Redis lets every instance of a service enforce one limit per user, API key or IP. The algorithm decides how bursty traffic may be and how much memory each key costs.

The four algorithms

Algorithm Redis structure Memory / key Burst behaviour Accuracy
Fixed window INCR + EXPIRE on rl:k1:{minute} 1 counter up to 2× limit across a window boundary coarse
Sliding log sorted set of timestamps one entry per request none exact
Sliding window counter two fixed counters, weighted 2 counters smoothed approximate (very close)
Token bucket hash {tokens, ts} 2 fields bursts up to bucket size, then steady rate exact

Fixed window's boundary problem

Sliding window counter estimates the rolling count as current + previous × (1 − elapsed fraction of current window): e.g. 30 s into the current minute with 40 now and 80 last minute → 40 + 80 × 0.5 = 80. Two integers per key, accurate enough for most APIs.

Token bucket in Lua (capacity C, refill r tokens/second) — the most common production choice because it allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate:

Lua
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key; ARGV: capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now      = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (math.max(0, now - ts) / 1000) * rate)
local allowed = tokens >= cost
if allowed then tokens = tokens - cost end

redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)   -- idle buckets disappear
if allowed then return {1, math.floor(tokens)} end
return {0, math.ceil((cost - tokens) / rate * 1000)}                    -- retry-after ms
Java
@Component
public class TokenBucketLimiter {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final RedisScript<List> script = RedisScript.of(new ClassPathResource("lua/token_bucket.lua"), List.class);
    public TokenBucketLimiter(StringRedisTemplate redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    /** @return empty if allowed, otherwise the retry-after duration */
    public Optional<Duration> tryAcquire(String apiKey, int capacity, double perSecond) {
        List<?> r = redis.execute(script, List.of("rl:tb:{" + apiKey + "}"),
                String.valueOf(capacity), String.valueOf(perSecond),
                String.valueOf(System.currentTimeMillis()), "1");
        long allowed = ((Number) r.get(0)).longValue();
        return allowed == 1 ? Optional.empty() : Optional.of(Duration.ofMillis(((Number) r.get(1)).longValue()));
    }
}

Design notes

  • Pass time from the client only if clocks are synced; otherwise use redis.call('TIME') inside the script (allowed since Redis 5 with effect replication) so all instances share one clock.
  • Fail open or closed? If Redis is unreachable, most APIs fail open (allow, log, alert) so a cache outage doesn't become a full outage; security-sensitive limits (login attempts, OTP) fail closed.
  • Return standard headers: RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After.
  • Layer limits: per IP at the edge (CDN/WAF), per API key at the gateway, per user per endpoint in the service, and a global concurrency limit (bulkhead) protecting the database.
  • Ready-made: Spring Cloud Gateway's RequestRateLimiter (Redis token bucket), Bucket4j with a Redis/Lettuce backend, Resilience4j RateLimiter (in-process only).

Interview tip in a system-design round, say which algorithm and why ("token bucket: allows bursts of 20, sustains 5/s"), where state lives (Redis, keyed per API key, Lua for atomicity), and what happens when Redis is down.

redis-spring.tldr:
• Configure JSON serializers, not JDK serialization.
  • Set per-cache TTLs with RedisCacheManager; @Cacheable(sync = true) coalesces local loads.
  • Lettuce is the default thread-safe client; always set a command timeout.
  • Store HTTP sessions in Redis with Spring Session for stateless app servers.
redis-spring.body:
YAML
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
      port: 6379
      timeout: 500ms                 # command timeout: always set one
      lettuce:
        pool: { max-active: 32, max-idle: 16, min-idle: 4 }   # requires commons-pool2
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 10m
      cache-null-values: false
Java
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class RedisConfig {

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory cf) {
        RedisCacheConfiguration defaults = RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
            .entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
            .disableCachingNullValues()
            .serializeValuesWith(RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair
                .fromSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));   // JSON, not JDK serialization

        return RedisCacheManager.builder(cf)
            .cacheDefaults(defaults)
            .withCacheConfiguration("products", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofHours(1)))
            .withCacheConfiguration("prices", defaults.entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public RedisTemplate<String, Object> redisTemplate(RedisConnectionFactory cf) {
        RedisTemplate<String, Object> t = new RedisTemplate<>();
        t.setConnectionFactory(cf);
        t.setKeySerializer(new StringRedisSerializer());
        t.setValueSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer());
        t.setHashKeySerializer(new StringRedisSerializer());
        t.setHashValueSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer());
        return t;
    }
}

@Service
public class PriceService {
    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "prices", key = "#sku", sync = true)   // sync: one loader per key per instance
    public Price price(String sku) { return pricingClient.fetch(sku); }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "prices", key = "#sku")
    public void invalidate(String sku) { }
}

Lettuce threading model. One Lettuce connection is thread-safe and multiplexes commands from many threads over a single socket (Netty), which is why Spring Boot doesn't pool by default. Add a pool only for blocking commands (BLPOP), MULTI/WATCH transactions or very high throughput. Always set a command timeout: a hung Redis must not hang your request threads.

Session storage: spring-session-data-redis stores HTTP sessions in Redis so any instance can serve any request (stateless app servers).

Clients: Lettuce (default in Spring Boot; Netty-based, thread-safe, one shared connection works well), Jedis (simpler, needs a pool), Redisson (high-level distributed objects and locks).

redis-ops.tldr:
• Diagnose with SLOWLOG, LATENCY DOCTOR, --bigkeys, --hotkeys, MEMORY USAGE.
  • Never run KEYS *; iterate with SCAN.
  • Secure with private networks, ACLs, TLS and disabled dangerous commands.
  • Wrap Redis calls in timeouts and a circuit breaker so outages degrade to the DB.
redis-ops.body:
Production topology checklist

Metrics worth alerting on: hit ratio (keyspace_hits / (hits + misses)), evicted_keys rate, used_memory vs maxmemory, connected_clients, replication offset lag, instantaneous_ops_per_sec, latency percentiles from the client side.

  • Latency: SLOWLOG GET 10, LATENCY DOCTOR, INFO commandstats. Watch for O(n) commands on big collections.
  • Big keys and hot keys: redis-cli --bigkeys, redis-cli --hotkeys (needs an LFU policy), MEMORY USAGE key. Split big keys (shard a hash into h:0..h:N), replicate hot keys or add a local cache.
  • Memory: INFO memory → used_memory, mem_fragmentation_ratio (> 1.5 suggests fragmentation; activedefrag yes).
  • Never run KEYS * in production; use SCAN 0 MATCH order:* COUNT 1000 iteratively.
  • Security: bind to private networks, enable ACLs (ACL SETUSER) and TLS, disable or rename dangerous commands (FLUSHALL, CONFIG, KEYS).
  • Client side: set connect and command timeouts, use connection pooling appropriately, and wrap Redis calls in a circuit breaker so a Redis outage degrades to DB reads instead of failing every request.

qa.q: Why is Redis single-threaded yet so fast?
qa.a: Everything is in memory, data structures are optimized, and an event loop with I/O multiplexing serves thousands of connections without context switching or lock contention. The bottleneck is usually network or memory, not CPU. Redis 6+ adds I/O threads for networking while command execution stays single-threaded, which also gives per-command atomicity for free.

RDB takes periodic point-in-time snapshots: compact and fast to restore, but you lose writes since the last snapshot. AOF logs every write: with everysec you lose at most about a second, at the cost of larger files and slower restarts. The hybrid (RDB preamble + AOF) is the common production choice.

qa.q: What eviction policy would you choose for a cache?
qa.a: allkeys-lru for general caches, allkeys-lfu when a stable set of hot keys matters more than recency. Set maxmemory explicitly. Use volatile-* only when Redis also holds non-cache keys without TTLs that must never be evicted.

qa.q: Explain cache penetration, breakdown and avalanche.
qa.a: Penetration: lookups for non-existent keys bypass the cache every time — cache null results briefly and use a Bloom filter. Breakdown: one hot key expires and a burst of misses hits the DB — rebuild under a mutex or use logical expiry. Avalanche: many keys expire at once or Redis fails — add TTL jitter, run Redis in HA, and protect the DB with circuit breakers and rate limits.

qa.q: How do you keep the cache consistent with the database?
qa.a: Cache-aside with "update the DB, then delete the cache key" after commit, plus TTLs as a safety net. For tighter consistency, invalidate from CDC events (Debezium) so every committed change evicts the key, or use delayed double delete. Accept eventual consistency, and don't cache data that needs strong consistency.

qa.q: How do you implement a distributed lock in Redis?
qa.a: SET key token NX PX ttl to acquire with a unique token and expiry; release with a Lua script that deletes only if the stored token matches. Use Redisson for lease renewal (watchdog) and reentrancy. For correctness-critical sections add fencing tokens, since failover or long pauses can let two clients believe they hold the lock.

qa.q: How does Redis Cluster distribute data?
qa.a: Into 16384 hash slots via CRC16(key) mod 16384; each primary owns a subset of slots and has replicas. Clients route by slot and follow MOVED/ASK redirects. Multi-key commands require all keys in the same slot, which hash tags ({user:42}) guarantee.

Sentinel provides high availability (monitoring and automatic failover) for a single primary dataset; it doesn't shard. Cluster shards data across multiple primaries and includes failover. Choose Cluster when data or write throughput exceeds a single node.

Partially. MULTI/EXEC is atomic in the sense that commands run sequentially without interleaving, and isolated, but there's no rollback if a command fails at runtime, and durability depends on persistence settings. Use WATCH for optimistic concurrency, or Lua scripts for conditional logic.

Pub/Sub broadcasts to currently connected subscribers with no persistence — missed messages are gone. Streams persist entries, support consumer groups, acknowledgements, pending-entry lists and reclaiming stuck messages, making them a lightweight reliable queue.

qa.q: How would you build a leaderboard?
qa.a: A sorted set with the score as the member's points: ZINCRBY on each score change, ZRANGE key 0 9 REV WITHSCORES for the top 10, ZREVRANK for a user's rank, and ZRANGEBYSCORE for score ranges — all O(log n).

qa.q: What happens when Redis runs out of memory?
qa.a: It applies the configured maxmemory-policy. With noeviction (the default), write commands fail with an OOM error while reads still work; with an LRU/LFU policy, keys are evicted to make room. Without maxmemory, the OS may OOM-kill the process.

qa.q: What are big keys and hot keys, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Big keys hold very large values or collections; operations and deletes on them block the single thread and they unbalance cluster memory. Hot keys receive disproportionate traffic and overload one node or slot. Detect with --bigkeys/--hotkeys/MEMORY USAGE; fix by splitting keys, UNLINK for deletion, local caching or replicating hot data.

qa.q: Why shouldn't you use KEYS in production?
qa.a: KEYS pattern scans the entire keyspace in one blocking O(N) operation, stalling every other client on that instance. Use SCAN with a cursor and COUNT, which iterates incrementally.

cheat.redis-cheatsheet:
Why Redis is fast: the execution model

  • One thread executes commands, so each command is atomic; I/O threads only handle networking.
  • One slow command (KEYS *, huge HGETALL, big DEL) blocks every client.
  • Use SCAN and UNLINK, keep values small.
  • Scale with sharding (Cluster), not threads.

Data structures and when to use each

  • Strings for values/counters/locks, hashes for objects, lists for queues, sets for uniqueness.
  • Sorted sets power leaderboards, delayed jobs and sliding windows.
  • HyperLogLog counts uniques in 12 KB; streams give consumer groups with acks.
  • Name keys service:entity:id, set TTLs on cache keys, avoid big keys.

Persistence: RDB, AOF and hybrid

  • RDB snapshots are compact but lose recent writes; AOF everysec loses at most ~1 s.
  • The hybrid (RDB preamble + AOF) is the usual production choice.
  • fork() for snapshots can spike memory via copy-on-write.
  • A pure cache may run without persistence.

Expiration and eviction policies

  • Keys expire lazily on access and actively by sampling.
  • maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru/allkeys-lfu for caches; noeviction makes writes fail when full.
  • volatile-* policies only evict keys with TTLs.
  • LRU/LFU are approximated by sampling.

Replication, Sentinel and Cluster

  • Replication is asynchronous; WAIT reduces but doesn't remove loss on failover.
  • Sentinel provides failover for one primary; Cluster adds sharding over 16384 hash slots.
  • Multi-key operations in Cluster need hash tags ({user:42}).
  • Choose Cluster when data or writes exceed one node.

Caching patterns

  • Cache-aside: read cache, load DB on miss, write DB then delete the key after commit.
  • Delete rather than update the cache to avoid ordering races.
  • Add TTL jitter; consider a small local cache in front for very hot keys.
  • Write-through and write-behind trade write latency against durability.

Cache failure modes: penetration, breakdown, avalanche

  • Penetration (missing keys): cache nulls briefly, Bloom filter.
  • Breakdown (one hot key expires): mutex rebuild or logical expiry.
  • Avalanche (mass expiry or outage): TTL jitter, HA Redis, protect the DB.
  • Cache and DB consistency is eventual; don't cache what must be strongly consistent.

Distributed locks with Redis

  • Acquire with SET key token NX PX ttl; release with a Lua compare-and-delete.
  • Redisson adds a watchdog that renews leases, plus reentrant and fair locks.
  • Failover and long pauses can break mutual exclusion: add fencing for correctness.
  • Keep the lock scope minimal.

Transactions, Lua scripts, pipelining and pub/sub

  • MULTI/EXEC runs commands together with no rollback; WATCH adds optimistic checks.
  • Lua scripts give atomic check-and-set logic; keep them short.
  • Pipelining cuts round trips but isn't atomic.
  • Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget; Streams persist with consumer groups.

Rate limiting with Redis: algorithms and implementations

  • Fixed windows allow 2× bursts at boundaries; sliding window counters fix that with two integers.
  • Token bucket allows short bursts up to capacity while enforcing an average rate — the common production choice.
  • Do check-and-consume in one Lua script so concurrent instances can't race.
  • Decide fail-open vs fail-closed per limit, and return 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit headers.

Spring Boot with Redis

  • Configure JSON serializers, not JDK serialization.
  • Set per-cache TTLs with RedisCacheManager; @Cacheable(sync = true) coalesces local loads.
  • Lettuce is the default thread-safe client; always set a command timeout.
  • Store HTTP sessions in Redis with Spring Session for stateless app servers.

Operating Redis in production

  • Diagnose with SLOWLOG, LATENCY DOCTOR, --bigkeys, --hotkeys, MEMORY USAGE.
  • Never run KEYS *; iterate with SCAN.
  • Secure with private networks, ACLs, TLS and disabled dangerous commands.
  • Wrap Redis calls in timeouts and a circuit breaker so outages degrade to the DB.
